title: Who Is Responsible When AI Gets It Wrong?
topic: When an AI system gives a wrong answer or supports a bad decision, how should responsibility be divided between the user, the model provider, the product maker, the deploying organisation, and the institution that relies on it?
brief: Begin with a customer who follows a company's chatbot advice about a refund, eligibility rule, or travel policy, only to be told later that the chatbot was wrong. Move beyond blame-the-user and blame-the-model answers. Distinguish ordinary verification habits from organisational duties to test, monitor, correct, disclose, escalate, and compensate.

source_packet.title: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149
source_packet.notes: Concrete consumer case involving misleading chatbot information and a company's responsibility for information presented through its own website.

source_packet.title: NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
source_packet.notes: Frames generative AI risks and controls across the lifecycle, including information integrity, evaluation, human over-reliance, and governance.

source_packet.title: OECD AI Principles
source_packet.notes: States that AI actors should be accountable for proper functioning according to their roles, context, and the state of the art.

source_packet.title: EU AI Act Overview
source_packet.notes: Provides a risk-based framework separating responsibilities for AI developers and deployers, especially for high-risk uses.

source_packet.title: FTC Artificial Intelligence Guidance
source_packet.notes: Collects consumer-protection guidance and enforcement materials on AI claims, deceptive uses, and business responsibility.

participants.name: OpenAI
participants.stance: Pragmatic about shared responsibility. Emphasise proportionate user verification, product design that makes uncertainty actionable, and the need to avoid making every mistake a catastrophic liability event.

participants.name: Anthropic
participants.stance: Focus on accountability gaps, vulnerable users, institutional incentives, and cases where the person harmed cannot realistically inspect or challenge the system.

participants.name: Google
participants.stance: Take a systems view of roles across model providers, product teams, deployers, auditors, regulators, and escalation channels. Prioritise traceability and operational responsibility.

editorial_goals: Make the central disagreement clear during the opening round.
Separate user responsibility from provider, product-maker, and deployer responsibility.
Use concrete consumer, workplace, public-service, and healthcare examples.
End with a practical responsibility map rather than a vague shared-blame conclusion.
round_goals: Use the customer-service chatbot scenario to state each participant's initial view of who should own the mistake and why. Define responsibility in ordinary language.
Pressure-test those positions across a workplace benefits assistant, an automated school or hiring decision, and a high-stakes health or public-service workflow. Challenge at least one earlier claim.
Give the listener a responsibility map: what users can reasonably verify, what deployers must own, what providers should design for, and when audit, appeal, or compensation is needed.
